query: Consider the following context: The ability to endure extreme corrosion in challenging environments is reduced in stainless steel. This can be addressed by appropriate surface modification techniques to redefine the surface with the required properties. In that context, which method can be used for improved corrosion resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning-driven optimization of coating composition and magnetron sputtering deposition parameters can significantly improve the corrosion resistance of stainless steel in harsh, corrosive environments by engineering a protective and uniform surface layer.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard stainless steel that exhibits reduced corrosion resistance under challenging conditions due to its unmodified surface.
generation.intervention: Application of a coating on the stainless steel surface using magnetron sputtering, where the deposition parameters (e.g., sputtering power, gas flow, multi-element ratios, and film thickness) and composition are optimized using a data-driven, machine-learning model.
generation.conditions: Exposure to extreme corrosive environments such as high-temperature or mixed-salt (e.g., molten salt) conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, dense, and homogeneous coating layer with tailored composition that forms a robust protective barrier on the stainless steel surface.
generation.mechanism: The optimized coating is expected to inhibit the underlying metal from direct exposure to corrosive agents by forming a stable and self-healing protective film. The data-driven approach enables rapid screening of composition and processing parameters to achieve the ideal microstructural features that block aggressive species and reduce galvanic micro-coupling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Stainless steel modified with the machine-learning-optimized coating will exhibit a lower corrosion rate and enhanced durability in extreme environments compared to uncoated or conventionally coated stainless steel.
generation.baseline: Standard stainless steel or stainless steel with non-optimized surface modification techniques.
generation.boundary: Effects are expected under conditions typical of extreme corrosion challenges (e.g., high temperatures and aggressive salt media). The performance improvements may vary with the specific corrosive medium and may not extend to environments significantly different from the testing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The degree of improvement in corrosion resistance and the optimal composition/process parameters require experimental validation. There is also uncertainty regarding the transferability of the optimized parameters across different corrosive environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of stainless steel samples with coatings deposited using magnetron sputtering. Divide them into two groups: one set with coating parameters optimized by the machine-learning model, and a control set with standard, non-optimized parameters. Expose all samples to a simulated harsh corrosive environment (e.g., high-temperature molten salt conditions) for a fixed duration.
measurements: Corrosion rate (via weight loss or electrochemical techniques such as potentiodynamic polarization)
Surface morphology and microstructural integrity using electron microscopy
Measurement of protective film uniformity and composition using surface spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine-learning-optimized coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate and improved mechanical/surface properties compared to the control coatings, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. decision.trend: Studies that discuss stainless steel in harsh chemical environments have done comparative corrosion tests or used new surface layers. One approach (PMC7304825) deposits a refractory high-entropy alloy film onto 304 stainless steel by magnetron sputtering to improve mechanical and tribological performance. Another (PMC6908586) examines corrosion of a high-entropy alloy alongside 316 stainless steel under severe molten salt conditions, highlighting potential dissolution issues with certain alloy elements. A third (PMC9955357) compares duplex stainless steel (2205) against a eutectic high-entropy alloy in a molten salt environment, observing that targeted compositions and protective layers can outperform standard stainless steels. While specialized coatings or novel alloy design can enhance corrosion resistance, systematically selecting optimal compositions and deposition parameters for each environment remains an open challenge.
decision.unsolved: It is not yet clear which specific coating compositions and processing routes most effectively protect stainless steel across diverse corrosive environments, especially under high temperature or mixed-salt conditions. Detailed, systematic optimization of coatings, accounting for composition, thickness, and deposition conditions, is still needed to ensure robust, long-term performance in real-world applications.
decision.lever: Use a machine-learning-driven optimization of coating composition and deposition parameters (e.g., magnetron sputtering power, gas flow, multi-element ratios, thickness).
decision.why: Advanced data analytics can rapidly screen vast composition and process variables to identify optimal surface modifications for stainless steels in challenging environments. By integrating experimental corrosion data into machine-learning models, researchers can efficiently pinpoint designs that maximize corrosion resistance, accelerating discovery and reducing trial-and-error in the lab.
